prize_parts.citation: for showing how collateral constraints tie credit to asset prices, so that small shocks are amplified and propagated into persistent economic fluctuations

statement.case_for: My configuration has changed. In round 1 I preferred B036 (Helpman, Melitz) and named B040 as my main alternative. After the exchange I now prefer B040 with Kiyotaki and Moore as a single part. The reason is merit and attribution, not the support counts. The chair asked which common criterion each member ranks first. Mine is a conceptual advance that is mature and cleanly attributable under a three-name cap. Kiyotaki and Moore (1997) isolate one general mechanism: borrowing limits tied to collateral value feed back on asset prices, so small shocks become large and persistent. After nearly three decades it is a standard building block in macro-finance, quantitative macro and policy models. The originating contribution sits with two people, and no co-originator is left out. B036 cannot say the same, because I conceded in round 1 that omitting Bernard, Eaton, Jensen and Kortum is its strongest reservation. The exchange also weakened the 2022 overlap objection that had kept B040 fifth in my opening ranking. Hassler, Andersson, Strömberg and Dreber-Almenberg separate bank runs, deposit insurance and bank failures from the collateral-value feedback loop in the real economy, and I find that distinction credible. I draw the citation around the mechanism and its influence, not around the size of the amplification. I do not see a viable multi-part configuration. No second part meets the same maturity and attribution standard without splitting credit, as the one-name B044 idea would. I therefore propose a single part.
statement.case_against: The most serious reservation is indirect empirical validation. As someone working on growth measurement, I am wary of crediting a mechanism whose quantitative importance is contested. Calibrated versions have, as far as I recall from general knowledge, often found weaker amplification than the stylised model suggests, and I have not verified this. The 2022 overlap is narrowed by the mechanism distinction but not eliminated, and I rest that on members' own descriptions, not on a check of the 2022 scientific background. Excluding Gertler and Gilchrist favours the theory over the more empirical financial-accelerator strand, as Dreber-Almenberg says, and the Committee should state that openly. The case also rests heavily on one seminal paper and its extensions, which looks narrow beside broader empirical programmes. My own field is macroeconomics, and I moved toward a macro candidate after earlier preferring a firm-reallocation one. I have tried to apply the same criteria to both.

responses.point: Hassler prefers B040 with the two originators and qualifies his opening wording. Only Bernanke among the accelerator authors is a laureate, so excluding Gertler and Gilchrist should rest on the independent origin and distinctness of the collateral-constraint mechanism, not on prior recognition. He also distinguishes the 2022 bank-run work from the collateral-value feedback loop.
responses.response: I accept the qualification and I have moved toward his position. In round 1 I noted that Krusell and I saw the 2022 prize narrowing the marginal case. I now think that overstated it. The distinction between bank runs and intermediation on one side and the asset-price and collateral feedback on the other is substantive. I would also base the exclusion of Gertler and Gilchrist on distinct origin, not prior recognition, and I would keep the pair. I do not accept that influence on quantitative and policy models alone settles durability. The indirect validation caveat belongs in the Committee's reasoning, and the citation should not claim a settled magnitude.

responses.point: Krusell has moved to B044 with Autor, Dorn and Hanson, anchored on trade-shock evidence. He grants B040 the cleanest attribution but places it just behind because empirical testing of collateral amplification is indirect and the 2022 prize narrows its marginal novelty.
responses.response: I agree with him on attribution. A three-author design with Dorn included is the right reading of the China-shock papers. I partly agree on indirect validation and put it first among my uncertainties. I differ in weighing a conceptual mechanism that reorganised how a field models credit above a credibly identified design whose magnitudes and persistence are still debated under shift-share inference. After the exchange I also read the 2022 overlap as narrower than he does. We differ in weighting, not in how we read the evidence, and I have moved B044 up into my alternatives.

responses.point: Enflo, like me a B036 supporter in round 1, names B040 as her first alternative. She concedes its attribution is cleaner than B036's, says she would not oppose it if the Committee weighs clean attribution above empirical grounding, and treats Bernard, Eaton, Jensen and Kortum as B036's real weakness.
responses.response: Her concession and mine point the same way, and I have acted on it. I still hold that Melitz-style selection is distinct from the trade work recognised in 2008, and I would keep B036 as an alternative. But we both concede the credit boundary with the firm-level co-originators is unresolved. Under a three-name cap that makes the citation less stable than B040's. I weigh that more heavily than I did in round 1, and I take her empirical-grounding point as the cost of choosing B040.

responses.point: Fredriksson prefers B044 with Autor, Dorn and Hanson and anchors the citation on empirical evidence about trade and technology exposure. He judges that a decade of replication refines the magnitudes without overturning the finding, and he asks the B040 supporters about overlap with recognised financial-frictions work.
responses.response: I agree that the trade-shock design is an unusually well-attributed trio and that a decade of replication across countries counts for a lot. The narrower citation also answers the worry about task-lineage authors outside the credited set. On his question, I find the mechanism distinction convincing: collateral values and asset-price feedback differ from the bank-run and bank-failure results recognised in 2022. I rank B040 first because it has had three decades of scrutiny and a purely conceptual claim, and the effect sizes in B044 are still contested. Neither point disqualifies B044, which is why I list it as an alternative.

responses.point: Dreber-Almenberg supports B040 and says the citation should rest on the mechanism and its influence on how crises are modelled, not on empirical confirmation of magnitudes. She adds that the Committee should state openly that leaving out Gertler and Gilchrist favours the theory over the tested evidence.
responses.response: I adopt that drafting approach in my citation. It avoids claiming more than the evidence supports, and it follows from the validation caveat that Andersson and others also raise. I also agree the cost of the two-name attribution should be stated. For me that cost is acceptable because the 1997 mechanism has an independent origin that the accelerator strand does not share. I would reconsider if a colleague showed that the quantitative-validation gap is wider than the mechanism's influence suggests.

uncertainties: How far the 2022 prize on banks and financial crises narrows the marginal case for Kiyotaki and Moore. I rely on members' descriptions of the mechanism difference, not on a check of the earlier scientific background.
How much weight indirect or mixed empirical validation of collateral amplification should carry against conceptual generality and demonstrated influence on models and policy.
Whether leaving out Gertler and Gilchrist undercredits the more empirical financial-accelerator strand, or correctly preserves a clean attribution to the originators.

Whether B044, with Autor, Dorn and Hanson and a citation anchored on trade-shock evidence, is judged a stronger single achievement. That turns on shift-share inference, persistence of the effects, and whether the task-based strand is a separate achievement.
Whether B036's omission of Bernard, Eaton, Jensen and Kortum, and the credit boundary for Helpman, would be resolved by the Committee in a way I have not anticipated.
My assessments rest on general knowledge and the supplied round-1 files, not on independent verification of citations, replication or impact.
statement.conflict_note: Updated for my new preference. None of the credited names on B040 (Kiyotaki, Moore, Gertler, Gilchrist) appears in my supplied profile as a co-author or institutional collaborator. I co-author with the secretary Per Krusell and the chair John Hassler, and am an IIES colleague of both. Hassler supports B040 and Krusell has moved to B044, and I disclose this without adjudicating it. I co-authored with Aghion, Bergeaud, Klenow and Li on creative-destruction growth measurement; none of them is credited on B040 or on my alternatives B036 and B044. Klenow is credited only on B006, which I do not propose. My research is in macroeconomics, the same broad field as B040. My earlier preference B036 was thematically close to my work on firm dynamics and reallocation. These ties are disclosed, not adjudicated.
